prompt: Roughly how often does a drop fall in the University of Queensland pitch drop experiment?
options: About once a decade
About once a year
About once a month
About once a century
explanation: Nine drops have fallen since the stem was cut in 1930, the first after eight years. Warmer pitch flows faster, so the gaps have varied.

prompt: The Oxford Electric Bell, ringing since 1840, is a true perpetual motion machine.
explanation: It runs on two dry piles, early batteries that deliver only a tiny current. It will stop when its clapper wears out or the piles run down.

prompt: The Beverly Clock in Dunedin is wound mainly by daily changes in air __________, which make the air in a sealed box push on a diaphragm.
explanation: A swing of about 4 degrees Celsius a day is enough, and changes in air pressure help too. The clock has stopped when the temperature stayed too steady.

prompt: What keeps the Oxford Electric Bell's little metal ball swinging between its two bells?
options: It picks up charge from one bell, is pushed away, and carries the charge to the oppositely charged bell
A clockwork spring that was wound once in 1840
Air currents from the laboratory's heating
A magnet that flips its poles twice a second
correctAnswer: It picks up charge from one bell, is pushed away, and carries the charge to the oppositely charged bell
explanation: The two dry piles hold the bells at opposite charges. Each trip moves only a tiny packet of charge, which is why the piles have lasted so long.

prompt: Match each person to their part in the slowest experiments:

pairs.right: Set up the Queensland pitch drop in 1927
Watched the pitch for 52 years without seeing a drop fall
Labeled the Oxford bell "Set up in 1840"
Built a clock in 1864 that the weather winds

explanation: All three experiments live in university physics departments, and the European Journal of Physics reported on them together in 1984.

prompt: What did Robert Wood secretly do during his 1904 visit to René Blondlot's laboratory?
options: Removed the aluminum prism, and Blondlot kept getting the same readings
Switched off the N-ray source halfway through
Swapped the phosphorescent screen for a plain one
Recorded Blondlot's results with a hidden camera
correctAnswer: Removed the aluminum prism, and Blondlot kept getting the same readings
explanation: Without the prism there was nothing to split the beam, yet the readings did not change. Wood also swapped a steel file for a wooden ruler, and the observer still reported the effect.

prompt: When OPERA reported in 2011 that neutrinos seemed to beat light, the team declared that Einstein's relativity had been overturned.
explanation: OPERA said the result was a complete surprise and asked for independent measurements. A faulty element in its fiber-optic timing system turned out to explain it.

prompt: A joint analysis with the Planck satellite showed that the BICEP2 signal came mostly from galactic __________, not from gravitational waves.
explanation: Dust grains in the Milky Way give off polarized microwaves. Planck's maps showed this dust glow was comparable to the BICEP2 signal even in the cleanest patches of sky.

prompt: Why could BICEP2 not rule out galactic dust on its own?
options: It observed at a single frequency, so it could not separate dust from the ancient light
Antarctic snow kept covering the telescope
Dust only shows up in visible light
It observed the whole sky at once and lost detail
correctAnswer: It observed at a single frequency, so it could not separate dust from the ancient light
explanation: Dust and the cosmic microwave background change brightness differently with frequency. Planck's nine frequency channels let the two be pulled apart.

prompt: Match each claim or test to what it really showed:

pairs.right: Observers seeing what they expected in faint glows
A faulty element in a fiber-optic timing system
Polarized dust in our own galaxy
Readings that did not depend on the apparatus

explanation: Each false discovery fell to an independent check: a hidden change to the apparatus, rival detectors with their own clocks, and a satellite that could see dust at many frequencies.

prompt: Le Grand K's official copies drifted away from it by tens of micrograms. Why could nobody tell whether the copies or Le Grand K itself had changed?
options: By definition Le Grand K weighed exactly one kilogram, so there was nothing better to check it against
The copies were never weighed again after 1889
Le Grand K was lost during the Second World War
Micrograms are too small for any balance to detect
correctAnswer: By definition Le Grand K weighed exactly one kilogram, so there was nothing better to check it against
explanation: Under the old system the prototype had zero uncertainty by law. If it lost atoms, the kilogram itself shrank, which is why the 2019 definition ties the unit to the Planck constant instead.

prompt: Méchain's hidden latitude error is the main reason the original meter came out about 0.2 millimeters short.
explanation: The shortfall came mainly from wrong assumptions about the Earth's exact shape. Because every later definition was matched to the one before, today's meter still carries it.

prompt: On a night with a leap second, official clocks read 23:59:59, then 23:59:__________, then 00:00:00.
explanation: That extra second keeps clock time within 0.9 seconds of the Earth's rotation. Twenty-seven were added between 1972 and 2016.

prompt: What did the world's metrology conference decide about leap seconds in 2026?
options: From 20 May 2027 UTC runs continuously, and clock time may drift up to an hour from Earth time
A negative leap second will be removed at the end of 2027
Leap seconds will be added every year from now on
The second will be redefined using the length of the day
correctAnswer: From 20 May 2027 UTC runs continuously, and clock time may drift up to an hour from Earth time
explanation: The 2022 conference had set 2035 as the deadline. The 2026 one brought it forward, partly because a never-tested negative leap second was becoming likely.

prompt: Match each name to what it describes:

pairs.right: Platinum-iridium cylinder that defined the kilogram until 2019
Weighs a mass against an electromagnetic force tied to the Planck constant
Astronomer who hid a discrepancy in his Barcelona latitude
Extra second that keeps atomic time close to the Earth's rotation

explanation: Each story is about the same move: trading physical objects and the spinning Earth for constants of nature that anyone can measure anywhere.

prompt: Why is the Amaterasu particle's origin such a puzzle?
options: Traced back, it points to the Local Void, where nothing seems powerful enough to have made it
It came straight from the Sun, which should be far too weak
Its energy was too low for any detector to measure
It arrived at exactly the same time as the Oh-My-God particle
correctAnswer: Traced back, it points to the Local Void, where nothing seems powerful enough to have made it
explanation: Particles this energetic should barely bend in magnetic fields, so their direction ought to point to the source. One 2026 idea is that ultraheavy nuclei could travel farther than protons.

prompt: A careful 2016 study by Burridge and Linden confirmed that hot water reliably cools to freezing faster than cold water.
explanation: They found no evidence of a meaningful Mpemba effect and showed that misplacing a thermometer by just 1 centimeter could fake one. A related effect has since been shown cleanly in colloids.

prompt: The claim that hot water can freeze faster than cold is named after the Tanzanian student Erasto __________.
explanation: His hot ice-cream mix froze first in 1963, and he published the result with Dr. Osborne in 1969. Aristotle, Bacon and Descartes had made similar claims centuries earlier.

prompt: In the 1993 experiments by Knight, Jaeger and Nagel, what mainly carried a large bead to the top of a shaken column of small ones?
options: A convection cycle that rises in the middle and sinks in a thin stream along the walls
Buoyancy, because the bead was less dense than the small grains
Static electricity built up by the shaking
Air blown in from the bottom of the container
correctAnswer: A convection cycle that rises in the middle and sinks in a thin stream along the walls
explanation: The big bead rides the rising current but is too wide for the narrow downward stream, so it gets stranded at the top. Simulations suggest the same sorting works on small asteroids.

prompt: Match each name to what it describes:

pairs.right: Utah detector that recorded the Oh-My-God particle in 1991
2021 cosmic ray that seems to come from the Local Void
Student whose hot ice-cream mix froze first
Small asteroid whose boulders may have been sorted by shaking

explanation: All three effects are easy to observe and still argued over: where the most energetic particles come from, whether hot water wins, and exactly how shaken grains sort.
